bullets: How to find speed from distance and time, read speed and acceleration off motion graphs, and tell distance apart from displacement
slides.heading: Motion: speed, velocity and graphs
slides.notes: Welcome everyone in and say: today we follow one athlete, one graph line and one runner who turns around, and learn to read motion like a story.

bullets: Calculate speed and velocity from distance, displacement and time
Read gradient as speed on a distance-time graph and as acceleration on a velocity-time graph, and area under a velocity-time graph as distance
slides.heading: What we will learn
slides.notes: Read the goals aloud and tell the class: keep these in mind, because the exit ticket at the end will ask you to do exactly these things.

bullets: A velocity-time graph runs flat for ten seconds - is the object parked, or still moving?
What does the flat line actually claim about the velocity?
slides.heading: Flat line - has it stopped?
slides.notes: Ask for predictions and take two or three answers without judging them yet; say: the graph scenes will settle it.

bullets: Speed is distance over time; velocity is speed with a direction, so it uses displacement, not distance
On a distance-time graph the gradient is the speed; on a velocity-time graph the gradient is the acceleration and the area underneath is the distance travelled
slides.heading: Speed, velocity and two graphs
slides.notes: Say this slowly, because it is the map for the whole lesson: first the two quantities, then the two graphs and what each one hides in its shape.

bullets: The athlete sprints along the track from 0 m to 100 m in 20 seconds
100 divided by 20 gives a speed of 5 metres per second - and because she ran right, her velocity is 5 metres per second rightwards
slides.heading: Velocity is speed with a direction
slides.notes: Narrate the scene as it plays: follow the athlete down the track and name the moment the direction turns her speed into a velocity.

bullets: The line climbs 120 metres in 60 seconds while a probe travels along it
The gradient triangle builds underneath: rise over run is 120 over 60, a steady speed of 2 metres per second
slides.heading: Distance–time graphs: the gradient is the speed
slides.notes: Narrate the scene as it plays: ride the probe up the line, then watch the triangle expose the gradient as the speed.

bullets: The line rises from 0 to 20 metres per second in 10 seconds, so its slope is an acceleration of 2 metres per second squared
The shaded area grows under the line as time passes - that area is the 100 metres travelled
slides.heading: Velocity–time graphs: slope is acceleration, area is distance
slides.notes: Narrate the scene as it plays: first read the slope as acceleration, then watch the area fill in and name it as distance.

bullets: The runner jogs 400 metres down the track, turns, and jogs back in 100 seconds total
Distance is 800 metres, so speed is 8 metres per second - but displacement is zero, so velocity is zero
slides.heading: Check the thinking
slides.notes: Narrate the scene as it plays: the outward and return legs cancel as displacement while the distance keeps counting up.

bullets: A distance-time line climbs 120 m in 60 s: speed = gradient = 120 / 60 = 2 m/s
The line is straight, so the speed never changes along the climb
slides.heading: Worked example: reading a steady climb
slides.notes: Work this on the board slowly: build the gradient triangle, divide rise by run, and say the units out loud.

bullets: A cyclist covers 300 metres in 50 seconds - find the speed, then say what else you need to call it a velocity
Then open the worksheet: one speed calculation, one flat-line trap and two graph readings
slides.heading: Your turn
slides.notes: Give three quiet minutes for the first task, take answers from the class, then set the worksheet going in pairs.

bullets: Four questions: a flat velocity-time line, a gradient reading, an area reading, and the out-and-back runner
Write one sentence: what does a flat line on a velocity-time graph really mean?
slides.heading: Exit ticket
slides.notes: Collect the tickets at the door; the first question revisits the trap head-on, so it shows straight away who still reads flat as stopped.
